utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Mr. Tieger, we have a new member?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Not precisely, Your Honour. But for the record, Alan Tieger, Patrick Hayden, and Iain Reid appearing for the Prosecution today, and Mr. Hayden will be calling the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Good to see you again, Mr. Hayden. Last week, during the cross-examination of Dr. Robert Donia, Mr. Karadzic asked Dr. Donia to look at a set of facts, a questionnaire relating to the secession of Slovenia and Croatia, and following a review of the documents, Dr. Donia stated that there were five or six assertions with which he could concur, if you remember. So in order to identify to which questions he answered positively, I think we need to record -- file that questionnaire in one way or another, exhibit it or file it as a filing. Do you have any observation, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was trying to think of both -- the most efficient manner of doing that, Your Honour. I mean, one expedient that occurs to me, of course, is simply identifying, with the agreement of the parties, the specific references that were the focus of the witness's response, and introducing those. I'm not sure that it is necessarily as useful to introduce the entirety of the document, which was basically excluded from the answer. So we'll be happy to work with the Defence to make sure that we've identified correctly the single reference or the few references to which the Court just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me deal with this first. At the time, the Chamber also asked the Prosecution to review the facts, and following its review, Ms. Edgerton submitted that most of them were irrelevant to the case against the accused, but that it was still looking at a number of matters that it considered may be relevant; I mean, the Prosecution. So speaking for myself, I'm of the opinion that the degree of relevance may be -- may vary depending upon the context in which it is needed; for example, whether it is in the stage of admitting documents, issuing a binding order pursuant to Rule 54 bis, taking a judicial notice of adjudicated facts, or for the purpose of the agreed facts. In particular regarding the agreed facts on background materials, although the relevance may be only marginal, the Chamber is of the view that it would be assisted and it will benefit from the progression of the case. So if the background matters, such as those discussed in the accused's list of facts, could be agreed by the parties. So I would expect that you would come back with some specific answers to those questions, and then I also recommend the accused to pursue that line of defence in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understood, Your Honour, with the single -- and just to make sure I understand it correctly, we'll pursue that course. I understand that the amount of time invested by either side to determine the accuracy of peripheral facts is affected by that, so -- that issue, so to the extent the Prosecution is in a position to readily identify the accuracy of some of those facts, I will certainly address that matter as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll see what you will come up with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My view in respect of this document is the following: I believe that it should be admitted in its entirety and it should be stated which facts were not confirmed by the expert witness, because that is information as well. This expert witness, Donia, simply had to know certain things, and he did not know them. Therefore, I believe what he did not confirm is also relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We were about to order the Registry to file your submission in its entirety, so that has been -- that will be resolved. And then for the next matter, shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session again. It concerns the -- yes, Mr. Tieger, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I didn't mean to interrupt the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was simply going to note that with respect to an issue raised at the end of last session, and with our understanding of the Court's encouragement, we will submit today the list of Assembly sessions referenced in Dr. Donia's reports, discuss that with Mr. Robinson, and we'll be providing that to the Court hopefully by the end of the day, to the Court, to the Registry, and of course to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. The last item is related to the sitting schedule at the end of this month, i.e., the week of 28th. So the Chamber will not sit on Friday, the 2nd of July, in that week. Instead, unless there's a serious objection, the Chamber is minded to sit on Monday instead, but starting at 3.00. Having said that, let's call the witness, let's bring in the witness. Yes, we can bring in the Defence expert as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, and that would be General Radovan Radinovic who will come in. If I can just ask you a question for clarification, when you said we'll be sitting at Monday, 3.00 p.m., is that Monday the 28th of June?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, 28th of June. We asked General Radinovic in order to deal with some confidential matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Philipps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Philipps, as we discussed, part of your evidence in this case will be submitted in writing, so let me first address some of the preliminary formalities associated with that submission. Have you previously testified as an expert witness before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Yes, I testified in the trial against General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And that was on the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the microphones be brought closer to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And that was on the 5th, 10th, 16th to 17th of July in 2002; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: In 2002, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And did you recently meet with representatives of the OTP to prepare a witness statement that amalgamated your testimony in the Galic case with observations relevant to the amended charts that you prepared for the purposes of this case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to review the statement that you signed on that day?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Yes, I went through the statement to have a look to make sure that it was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And I believe there's a single correction that you wish to make that to statement. Mr. Registrar, if I could have 65 ter 90179, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the microphones be lowered closer to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If we could turn to page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are hearing French. I think it's resolved. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down to the second paragraph on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And in the second-to-last sentence, you state: "I am able to identify the main command post of the corps ..." Should that read "I am able to identify the rear command post"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Yes, that should be "the rear command post of the corps."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And in the second -- I apologise. In the last sentence of that paragraph, you state: "I am able to identify the forward command post ..." Should it be "the main command post"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: To be correct, it should be "the main command post of the corps."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: With that correction, Mr. Philipps, can you confirm that the statement is accurate, and that if you were asked the same questions on the same topics today, your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Yes, the statement is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in those circumstances, I tender 65 ter 90179, the statement of Mr. Philipps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. If I can just raise an issue with respect to this. You've held previously, in the decision on Prosecution's motion for admission of evidence of eight experts pursuant to Rules 92 bis and 94 bis, on 9th of November, 2009, that Rule 94 bis is lex specialis to Rule 92 bis, and therefore you didn't allow the procedures for Rule 92 bis to be followed. We now have the issue whether Rule 94 bis is lex specialis to Rule 92 ter. I am not sure that it makes a practical difference and I don't expect it is useful for us to make the Prosecution ask questions of the witness orally, but it seems like since it might be an issue that may have some impact on the jurisprudence, I think our position would be that we should treat his amalgamated witness statement as a report pursuant to Rule 94 bis and admitted on that basis. But I just raise that as a more technical issue than anything that we strenuously object to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. As a matter of practice, the Prosecution is able to present the expert report without asking any questions, even pursuant to Rule 94 bis. So if you agree. So in that case, given the jurisprudence that 92 ter evidence is similar to the evidence which is given viva voce, so speaking for myself, I don't see any problem. But if Mr. Hayden has any observation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I would only note, Your Honour, that in the decision that this Trial Chamber rendered in November last year concerning those eight 92 bis witnesses, it was noted that 94(b) is lex specialis to the situation where a witness doesn't attend. But, of course, in this situation we have the witness present in the courtroom, and it may be distinguished. I would also note in that decision the Trial Chamber instructed the Prosecution that it, indeed, may call those eight witnesses pursuant to 92 ter rather than 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. To be safe, I will confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is unanimous in admitting this document pursuant to Rule 92 ter, which will be given the Exhibit number as ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P989, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I will now read a brief summary of the evidence contained in that statement. Mr. Philipps is a former intelligence officer of the British Army. He held the rank of lieutenant-colonel. Since 1985, he has undertaken various training in military intelligence and analysis at Sandhurst and other British military academies. He served full-time as an intelligence officer during the first Gulf War and with SFOR in Sarajevo. From 2000 until 2006, he was employed as a military analyst by the Office of the Prosecutor. Using VRS documentation and other documentation, Mr. Philipps has reconstructed the structure of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, also known as the SRK, for the period from the corps' formation in May 1992 until the end of 1995. Mr. Philipps has depicted this structure on two charts, employing a standard format used by NATO. The charts show the corps commander at the top of the chain of command. The corps commander is supported by a corps operational staff, including a chief of staff, who was also known as the deputy corps commander. Subordinated to the corps command were brigades as well as the corps supporting units. The troops of the corps supporting units, which included artillery regiments, were directly subordinated to the corps commander, while each brigade had its own troops. The chart also shows the personnel in charge of each formation, unit, and sub-unit over the indictment period. In addition, Mr. Philipps has reviewed approximately 50 SRK-related documents, which are listed in Appendix A to his statement, and he has explained how these documents fit within the SRK chain of command and chain of reporting. That concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Philipps, we see before us in the courtroom two charts which, for the record, are 65 ter numbers 10590, at pages 1 and 2. The first chart on the easel in front of you bears the heading "Sarajevo Romanija Corps, VRS, 1992 to 1994." The second chart just behind you is dated August 1994 to 1995. Did you prepare these charts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Yes, I did prepare the charts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And what sources did you rely upon in preparing these charts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Primarily, the sources used to prepare the charts were documents from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. These consisted of orders, instructions, combat reports, and instructions to the corps from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Do you consider your review and use of SRK documents to be exhaustive of all the SRK documentation in the OTP archives?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: No. There are many, many documents from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and so I was only able to select and go through a part of those documents. And I specifically was looking for documents that related to the organisational structure of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And when you were reviewing those documents, in addition to focusing on information about the organisation and structure, did you review those documents for any other substantive information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: I was mainly looking at the structure, but also at command and control of the corps. But I didn't go into any detail on other matters relating to the actual combat. I was merely looking at the structure and the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Now, in your Galic testimony, you refer to the fact that you had relied upon documents purporting to be SRK documents that were disclosed by the Defence in that case. And for the Trial Chamber's reference, this is at page 3 of the statement. Subsequent to the Galic case, have you had an opportunity to verify the reliability of those documents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Yes, I've been able to compare those documents to documents directly from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and been able to establish that those documents provided by the Defence in Galic were, in fact, genuine Sarajevo Romanija Corps documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: With respect to documents not produced by the SRK, what other types of documents did you rely upon in constructing these charts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: The other main document that I relied upon was an instruction to the 4th Corps of the JNA. This was a document relating to how a corps should be run, the structure of the headquarters of that corps, and the tasks that a corps should undertake. That document outlines the structure of a headquarters and the staff required to run a headquarters of a corps in the JNA. That document was subsequently used by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps in its formation and in its methods of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Now, in terms of -- and, Mr. Registrar, if I can ask for 65 ter 02266, please. Do you have a document before you, Mr. Philipps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And is this the same document you refer to from the 4th Corps of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Yes, those are the instructions to the 4th Corps Command on carrying out priority assignments in peacetime and wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And just briefly, you have touched upon this, but what was the relationship between the JNA 4th Corps and the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: In a sense, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was formed from the remnants of the 4th Corps of the JNA. Many of the units within the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, in fact, bore the same name as the units that had been previously in the 4th Corps of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I'd ask for the admission of this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P990.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Turning to the charts, Mr. Philipps, in terms of what is depicted on there, and specifically in terms of the lower-level units or sub-units, such as infantry platoons, do you consider the chart to be a comprehensive reflection of all such SRK units?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: No. To produce a chart that showed every platoon and every company within a corps would make a chart so complex as to be unusable in that sense, so the chart concentrates on headquarters, formations, that is, brigade-sized units, and the battalions that made up those brigades. Occasionally, numbers of companies and companies are shown, and on some occasions, where relevant, a platoon is shown, but most of the detail down to company and platoon level is not shown on the charts --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And in the same respect, do you consider it to be a comprehensive reflection of all heavy weaponry; for example, various calibre mortars and guns attached to SRK units?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: No. Where I found evidence of particular weaponry, heavy weaponry or mortars and other types of heavy weapons, I included them in the chart, but it is by no means a comprehensive list of all the heavy equipment, including infantry support weapons, that were present in the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: You discuss in detail the methodology you employ in depicting the structure, particularly at pages 6 to 8 of your statement. I'd now like to just clarify a few aspects of that methodology. And if we can turn to Sanction, we may be able to zoom in on the detailed chart. At various points of the chart, we see both unbroken and broken lines running between the boxes; for example, on the first chart, the broken line running to the Engineer Unit within the Igman Infantry Brigade. What is the significance of the use of the unbroken line versus a broken line?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Where I found two or more documents that confirmed the existence of a unit, I used an unbroken line, that is, a solid line. Where only one document was located, that is, unconfirmed by the sources, then I've used a dotted or dashed line to indicate that there was no other source, simply a single source, to show the existence of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: We also see such broken lines depicting boxes; for example, on the first chart, the broken line which forms the Morale Division headed by Radomir Visnjic within the corps operational staff on the screen in front of you. Does the broken line have the same significance in this situation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: I don't have it on the screen in front of me, but I know what you're referring to from the main chart. Thank you, I can now see that. Again, this dotted line around the Staff Division for Morale relates to the existence of only a single document indicating the existence of that staff division.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: On the chart, we also see you have employed two different types of broken lines for the boxes depicting the formations. For want of a better description, one line is broken up less frequently, while the other may be described as a finely-dotted line. For example, if we look in the co-operation staff and the boxes there depicting the office computer section and so on, what's the significance of the use of the finely-dotted line?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: The dotted line shows part of the organisation that should exist in the All Bat [phoen] based on the 4th Corps instructions or is very likely to exist, the artillery staff being an example, where we do have artillery staff officers, but I have no reference to an artillery staff organisation. So where the dotted line is used for an organisation, it means that you would expect to find that part of the organisation there, but I have no specific document, other than a general instruction, that such a unit should exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the Ilijas Brigade depicted on the first chart, or if we look more generally at the units depicted in the chart, we see that there is -- there are the letters "VP" followed by a number in the top left-hand corner. What do those letters signify?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: The VP number was a method used by the VRS to identify specific units, so no two units would have the same VP number. This means that a VP number would be allocated to the corps, and formations within the corps would also be allocated VP numbers, and each of the battalions within those brigades would have VP numbers, down to the lowest level. So I can see we're zooming in to the Ilijas Brigade, and you can see that each unit and sub-unit within the Ilijas Brigade has its own VP number which consists of four numbers, a stroke, and then two other numbers, and this clearly identified each individual unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Looking at the units of the Ilijas Brigade, we see one of the units there entitled "Vasko's platoon." Firstly, who do you understand Vasko to be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Simply from the documents that list the VP numbers, "Vasko" appeared to just be the nickname or the name given to the commander, and so the platoon that he commanded was simply "Vasko's platoon." His name is actually listed on the chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Philipps, what does "VP" actually mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it stands for "Vojni Post," which is "Military Post."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: On what basis would you have attributed a VP number to Vasko's platoon?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: With reference to a specific document that listed the VP numbers of the Ilijas Brigade, and included in that list of VP numbers was Vasko's platoon, with an allocated number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And, specifically, what does the existence of a VP number assigned to Vasko's platoon indicate to you about its relationship to the SRK command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: It indicates to me that that platoon was part -- was under the command of the brigade, and that brigade was under the command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, so that platoon forms an integral part of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and is under the command and control of the corps through the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: On some parts of the chart, you've employed the term "temp attached" or "temp at." For example, if we look under the 1st Romania Infantry Brigade on the first chart, we look at the fourth row of subordinated units, and there we see a box within which is written: "MUP strength, 150. 25 May 1993. Temp at," and we see a Milko Koriman [phoen]" in that box. Firstly, is "temp attached" or "temp at" short for "temporarily attached"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I simply used that abbreviation there to fit it onto the chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And what does the term mean in the context of this example?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: A document existed that showed that a MUP unit with that listed strength of 150 was attached to that brigade for a specific operation. The attachment of the MUP might put the MUP under the control of that unit, but not necessarily under the command of the officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have 65 ter 11711. And we --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Can you see a document before you, Mr. Philipps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: This document we see before us is dated 17th of June, 1992. Looking at the first page before you, who is the recipient of the document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: The document is directed to the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And if we can turn to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Who is the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: The author of the document, that is, the individual writing the report, was the then commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, that is, Colonel Tomislav Sipcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And returning to the front page, if we scroll down to paragraph 4, and this paragraph begins: "Ilidza MUP ...," followed by: "They are mopping up the Akif Seremet and Georgi Dimitrovi. Streets. They engaged a small number of people. Instead of 210, estimated, they put into action around 40 people and some SRS volunteers who were are under their command." And it lists the casualties. According to your reading of this document, what is the relationship between the MUP, the SRS volunteers and the SRK during this combat operation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: The MUP appears to have the SRS volunteers under its command, from what is stated by Colonel Sipcic, and the MUP itself is operating within the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and that is why that information is being reported up the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If I can tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Philipps. Who is reporting to who in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The corps commander, Tomislav Sipcic, is reporting to the Main Staff, that is, the army headquarters of the VRS. So he's reporting from the corps up the chain of command to the general headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. At the time, the VRS has a different name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It all -- well, it -- there are various terms used for the army, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because I didn't follow the GS of the SRBH Army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the "GS" is the General Staff, and the SRBH refers to the Army of Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So the "VRS" and the "SRBH" are the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P991.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If I can be of assistance there, Your Honour, you can see in the English translation "GS" is followed by "Main Staff."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If we can call up 65 ter 12445.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: This is a document dated 16th of September, 1992. Just from the front page there, Mr. Philipps, can you tell us generally what kind of document this is and where it fits in in the chain of reporting?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: This is a report from a brigade commander, in this case the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade up the chain of command to the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And approximately halfway down the page, it reads: "The police agreed to all our demands for unified action and armed combat and, among other things, was involved in safe-guarding some of the positions of the Ozrenska Street front-line." Is this an example of the police units working in the area of responsibility of the SRK Command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Yes, this report from the brigade commander up the chain of command is reporting on co-operation with the civilian police, and particularly in this case mentioning a position on the front-line where the police appear to be acting in conjunction with the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And if we look at the paragraph immediately below that one, it reads: "Manpower levels of the brigade command consisted of 80 per cent senior officers already at the beginning and subsequently reached 90 per cent, whereas manpower levels of the battalion commands are 100 per cent, including all key command positions, which guarantees successful command in all the units, and we really do not face any problems with command and control in the units in combat." What does this aspect of the report tell you about the nature of command and control of one of the SRK brigades in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Well, in this case it does appear that the majority of the command posts are being filled by officers with the appropriate level of training, and only in the brigade command, itself, is there a lack of manpower of trained officers of about 10 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P992, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Philipps, in light of your experience in the military, and after your review of the collection of SRK documents, what conclusions did you draw about the overall nature or functioning of the command and control structure of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Over the period shown in the charts, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps appeared to run an effective command and control of the units, from formation level, that is, brigade, down through battalions, down to companies, down to platoon level. So the company commanders were able to report up the chain of command to battalions, battalions could report up to brigades, and brigades wrote detailed reports to the corps command, and information passed in the other direction. Further to that, the corps command were able to report those details to the Main Staff, that is, the Main Staff of the VRS, and the Main Staff were able to instruct the corps on its activities. This shows an effective command and control of the corps through the period, with accurate reporting, well-written reports with appropriate details.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes the examination-in-chief. I would now ask that the documents associated with Mr. Philipps' 92 ter statement, which include both the charts before us, be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So let's take one by one. The chart, are you tendering it as -- tendering two charts as an associate exhibit of his 92 ter statement, or, itself, is it an expert report, itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we consider it the expert report. It was -- the charts were listed in the 94 bis notification that was filed last year. Whatever the technicalities of admission, if it's more appropriate under Rule 94, then that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First, we'll admit those two charts as his expert report. We give them separate numbers. Let's do that first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 993 will be the chart which refers to the years from 1992 to 1994. And then we'll give the Exhibit P994 for the second chart which deals with the year from 1994 to 1995. And, Mr. Hayden, you also said that you would tender the note or seven-page report, as well as the list of units and list of personnel, as associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Again, those three documents were listed in the 94 -- Rule 94 bis notification. If it's more appropriate to submit them as expert reports, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That would be part of his expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: The note is an explanation of the charts. The two other documents, the indices that list the relevant underlying documents, we don't seek to tender those or all of those underlying documents as exhibits. But if it would be helpful for the Chamber to have those indices, then we submit those for evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And about the appendix, Appendix A, so you are tendering that also as a kind of appendix to his expert report, not necessarily as an associated exhibit, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: The appendix lists I think it's 47 documents -- 48 documents that we wish to tender into evidence. The appendix was considered part of his 92 ter statement. Again, if the more appropriate vehicle is Rule 94 bis, then we're happy to tender it under that Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll consider that the Appendix A as part of his 92 ter statement. So having said that, we'll admit separately his note and list of units and, finally, the list of personnel. We give three numbers to those.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. 65 ter 11553 will be Exhibit P995. 65 ter 10592 will be Exhibit P996. And 65 ter 10593 will be Exhibit P997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And, finally, we'll come to those 48 documents dealt with in his Annex A. So I would like to recall our guide-line which was given in our decision which was issued on 20th of October last year. I will quote: "Expert reports generally should be complete and understandable in themselves, such that there's no need to tender for admission into evidence the sources used by the expert. However, should the presenting party wish to tender certain sources used by an expert in compiling his or her report, it can reapply to the Chamber for the admission either orally or in writing. The Chamber notes that the presenting party should be very selective in the sources that it tenders for admission into evidence and provide clear reasons as to why these sources should be admitted in addition to the expert report, itself." In the case of Dr. Donia, the Chamber was very pleased to admit those sources. But in relation to these 48 documents, there are certain documents as to which the Chamber is not quite satisfied as to its relevance or necessity or in what context it is used in his report. So I will name those documents. Which will be convenient, in the order filed in the Annex A or in the order of alphabetical number -- no, numerical number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Whichever pleases you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then I will give the numbers in the order of numbers. These are all 65 ter numbers: 1643, 1864, 9035, 9273, 9383, 9469, 10693, 10931, 10932, 11286, 11657, 12178, 12182, 12199, 12202, 12377, 12380, 12383, 12400, 12402, 12407, 12409, and 12418. The Chamber is satisfied, with the relevance and the context, in admitting the remaining documents, so as for the main documents, at this moment the Chamber does not admit them at this moment. So you may come back with the full explanation or you may go through either of them with the witness at the end of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If I understand your instructions, Your Honour, we have the opportunity to present to you in writing the relevance of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In writing or you can go through them with the witness if you prefer. Of course, the Defence will be allowed to cross-examine in relation to the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I think we'll take the opportunity to submit something in writing. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Registry will circulate the status of the exhibit in writing in due course. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to all. Allow me to introduce Professor Dr. Radovan Radinovic, lieutenant-general, retired, who is assisting me in working with Prosecution experts for military matters. I would also like to thank Mr. Philipps for being so kind as to meet up with the Defence. We did meet yesterday at the Detention Unit, and we looked at certain matters that we may agree upon in order to save time for the Trial Chamber and for all of us. So thank you, Mr. Philipps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what I'd like to ask you: As the distinguished Prosecutor said, you are a military intelligence officer; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: I'm a retired military intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how one becomes a military intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Intelligence is simply a specialism within the army. So one can become an intelligence officer or an engineer officer or an artillery officer, and at the beginning of one's career one chooses the specialism, and I, by chance, chose intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What kind of schools need to be completed for that occupation, as it were?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: In the British Army, all officers receive the same basic training to become infantry officers so that they're capable of commanding troops on the battle-field, and later on they specialise into certain areas. I was commissioned into the Intelligence Corps after a course at the Military Academy in Sandhurst in 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that a military intelligence officer has to be familiar with all the other things that other military officers are taught during the course of their military education?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: At the beginning of the training, all officers are trained to the same level, to the same capability of being infantry officers, but then comes the training -- the specialist training. So I would not have the knowledge of, for example, a specialist engineer officer or a specialist artillery officer. I'm an intelligence staff officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, as far as military theory and doctrine is concerned, you are all equally familiar with that; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Yes, I've been trained to a certain level in military doctrine. Specifically having been an intelligence officer, I focused on combat intelligence, that is, really, the capabilities of the enemy, in terms of the British Army. So at that time that was considered to be the Soviet Union, so a lot of my work was studying the tactics, strategy, and capabilities of the Soviet Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that at every point in time, a particular army has an assumed enemy or a preferred enemy, and that then the army adjusts its doctrine and procedures accordingly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: The British Army studies other armies all the time. It specifically studies those armies which are at that time a threat. And in 1985, there was no doubt, in a sense, with the existence of the inner German border, that there was a concern that there might be a conflict with the Soviet Union. An army might change the armies that it studies over time. It's a very natural thing to study potential enemies as well as existing enemies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you permitted to tell us how things stand now in relation to the British Army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: I retired in 2006, so I have no current knowledge of what the British Army might consider to be the enemy. But the British Army is currently fighting in Afghanistan, so a great deal of intelligence work, for example, would be going on relating to the Taliban and the structures and capability of the Taliban. But that is something that is really general knowledge and not specific knowledge to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So Karadzic is not being taken into consideration at all in the British Army as a potential enemy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: I really couldn't say, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, you've included some 50 documents. You've had a look at all the documents involved, but you studied some 50-odd documents of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: The references to my report show that I've included several hundred documents in compiling the report, but not all of those are tendered as exhibits, as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the information in your report has, as its source, all of these documents that are listed, not only those 50-odd documents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Yes, the charts both have indices relating to personnel units and equipment, and these indices list all the documents that I used to extract data from to create the charts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any reports that you had not taken into account?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: There are many, many documents of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps that I have not read and not been through. There is often, when preparing a report like this, insufficient time to read every available source. It would have taken many, many years to produce a report if I'd been through every available document. I had to be selective.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was it that carried out that selection, you or the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: I selected which documents were appropriate to be referenced in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have in mind any particular request of the Office of the Prosecutor or a specially profiled task, as it were?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: The task I was originally given was by Mr. Ierace to prepare the charts for the Galic case, and his directive was to prepare an organisational chart showing the structure, command and control of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, but it didn't extend into any other details. When I was re-tasked to produce the updated reports for this case, a similar set of instructions were given to update the organisational structure, to update any further information we had from additional SRK documents relating to command and control and structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So there are some differences between your first report and testimony and this report; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Yes, there will be some small differences. The time-period means that the chart was split into two different periods. And, furthermore, additional information was available from original SRK documents which by then had come into the hands of the OTP, and they were then given to me to select.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what is the specific difference involved in relation to the first insight you had?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is different in the new report as compared to your old report? Did it change your view of this corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: The additional information really provided extra detail on certain units, extra information to show when those units existed or when they changed or changed their names. It provided information on units that were formed after 1994. The documents provided additional information on reporting in the chain of command, additional information on combat reporting, strengths of the units, the type of ammunition and, therefore, the type of weapons used. So as I worked through the documents, I was able to, you might say, improve the reports as regards detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you said that you were a specialist in assessing combat readiness and capacities, did you assess the Sarajevo Romanija Corps from that point of view as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: I did not assess the combat effectiveness or combat readiness of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. I really only assessed the command and control capabilities of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the Office of the Prosecutor have certain suggestions or instructions in relation to the conclusions to be drawn in respect of combat effectiveness and command and control capabilities of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps? In other words, did you know what the objective of the OTP was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I was simply given instructions to put together an organisational chart and look at the command and control and reporting. I wasn't given any information about their pre-trial brief. I haven't read the pre-trial brief. I haven't read the indictment. All I'm doing is presenting the structure of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. So there was no agenda, if you like, from the OTP that was given to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It doesn't have to be a hidden agenda of any kind. But, anyway, Mr. Philipps, I would be interested in the following: The structure of this kind of an operative unit like a corps, I mean its functioning, does it depend on the tasks before it? Is that task of relevance? And in relation to that task, does one assess whether things are sufficient, insufficient, exaggerated, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: The concept of the structure and command and control of a corps is such that it is able to fulfill a certain set of tasks or operations, and it should, with that structure, be capable of fulfilling the set of tasks such as those laid out in the 4th Corps instructions. You would not expect to keep changing the organisation of a military unit just because the tasks put before it changed. Certainly at the corps level, it's expected to have the capability to fulfill those tasks. Having said that, when circumstances change, it may be necessary to change the structure of an organisation, the relationship between the numbers of troops, the number, for example, of engineers or artillery. So the answer would be: Generally, a corps would have a certain structure to fulfill its tasks, but may be changed over a period of time as those tasks develop, whereas the military situation changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I believe that the development of the military situation is significantly affected by the other party that is at war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: The -- any military situation of conflict, inevitably the activities of the enemy influence the capabilities of -- capabilities and structure and organisation of any military unit that is fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So do you agree that it would have been a good thing if we had had more insight as far as the enemy was concerned or, rather, the other warring party that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was facing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question. Are you talking about currently or historically?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no. I'm talking about the time when the Sarajevo Romanija Corps existed. Do you agree that its functioning, its structure, effectiveness, the measures that it took, et cetera, were largely dictated and tested by the enemy, and these are exams that one cannot re-sit, as it were?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: The structure of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps gave it, for example, an intelligence and security division at the corps staff level. Every combat report that came up to the corps headquarters, the first paragraph would cover the actions of the enemy. The purpose of the corps in fighting would be to avoid being pushed, if you like, to avoid being directed into certain actions by the enemy. The purpose of fighting is to prevent the enemy from directing you into course of action. So there was a detailed intelligence flow from the units on the front-line to the command and from the command up to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the time be right for the break or should I go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, if it is convenient, it's time to take a break. We'll break for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could move very briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was advised that the morning slot is empty on Friday, so we would prefer to sit in the morning this week, Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry for the inconvenience, Mr. Philipps and Mr. Radinovic. Mr. Karadzic, shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Philipps, are you familiar with our situation as a whole; primarily, the Yugoslav situation as a whole, but also the Bosnian crisis, specifically?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Are you referring to the conflict in Yugoslavia during the period of the charts?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: I have a little knowledge of that, of the events that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to suggest that we go through the points that we agreed upon considerably during our interview so that we can leave that ad actum. Do you agree that at a certain point in time, the JNA was very powerful? Some people even say it was the fourth-strongest army in Europe?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I was never an expert on the JNA, and so I'm not capable of ranking it in terms of strength or capability at that time in history.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you do agree that it was the only military force in Yugoslavia and that the recruitment base was a population of 22 million; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Again, I wouldn't know what the population of Yugoslavia was in the 1990s. I understand that the JNA was recruited from entirely within the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We agreed yesterday that all the officers and the entire reserve force was related to Yugoslavia, was trained in Yugoslavia and belonged to the JNA, as such; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Many of the officers shown on the chart -- on the two charts behind me were trained JNA officers and trained JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We agreed that the officers of the armies of the other republics, Slovenia, Croatia, the Muslim army, et cetera, that a large number of them -- or, actually, all the officers could only come from the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Again, I haven't studied the composition of those other forces. But as I understand it from what I've read and what I've been told, there were also trained officers from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that some of them had served in the JNA all the way up until the conflict started?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Yes. Most certainly from the point of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, which I have looked at in detail, the officers were professional full-time serving officers, or at least some of those officers were full-time officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in the armies of the other republics, they also got their own officers who until then had been professional officers in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Again, the other armies involved in the conflict haven't been a subject of my study. But if -- it seems likely that they were trained JNA officers. I'm not sure that I'm the person to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that there had been no other army but the JNA and that all the reservists were JNA conscripts in all the republics?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Again, I'll have to qualify my answer, not having studied the other armies. The SRK certainly consisted of JNA -- former JNA conscripts and reservists, and one might assume, therefore, that the other armies consisted of the same types of troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that war is always waged with a purpose or objective?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: That's almost a philosophical question, outside my abilities. War is waged for all sorts of reasons, and I wouldn't want to make a general statement about war, through history, that I haven't studied in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It would be nice to think that it was, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that -- with a maxim that when two laws or two rights clash, that a solution can usually be found only in war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, where are we going?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, let us see why the Sarajevo Romanija Corps existed in the first place. Let us see why that army existed in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If that is too general a question for you, then I'm going to move on. Do you agree that that corps had a certain military task, a certain area of work, and certain objectives?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Yes, it would appear that the corps was given military instructions, it was given an area of responsibility, and it was given military objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said yesterday, during our interview, that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps had been established under strange circumstances during the war and on an ad hoc basis; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: The Sarajevo Romanija Corps was formed when the conflict had already started, and any organisation formed during a conflict does not have a straightforward formation at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I tell you that the objectives of the warring parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina, taking into account primarily the Serbs and Muslims here because we are discussing Sarajevo, the objective of the Muslim side was to prevail throughout Bosnia and to have 100 per cent authority in Bosnia, and the objective of the Serb side was for Bosnia to remain in Yugoslavia, and if Bosnia would not remain in Yugoslavia, then they would get their own constituent unit within Bosnia? Does that sound familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: You're talking at the political level, and my knowledge is of the military level, and so I can't really answer that question. I don't know what the objectives of the Bosnians were or the objectives of the Serbians were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While studying combat documentation of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, did you manage to glean, as it were, what the objectives of that corps were?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Are you asking me whether there's a specific instruction to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps? As far as I understand it, I did see such an instruction, but I would be hard pressed to recall it exactly without the document in front of me, and I don't remember which document it was. The objective appeared to be the blockade of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have to go through the documents together. We agreed that you don't have much knowledge about the 1st Corps of the BH Army, but that you believe it might have had the same structure as the Sarajevo Romanija Corps because they stem from the same school; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: In a sense, all military organisations are similar. Whatever period of history you look at, military formations have a similar organisation. Having been formed from officers and soldiers of the JNA, if that's what you've been saying, then the ABiH may very well have had a similar structure, but I haven't studied it. So, in a sense, I'm the wrong person to ask, not being an expert on the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we have in e-court 1D01892, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for it to come up, Mr. Philipps, I'd like to tell you that it's a similar chart, and it originates from the Muslim army. The boxes are not spread out in the same way, they are placed one underneath the other, but if you would look at this and tell me whether it looks convincing and realistic to you. It seems we'll have to have it on the ELMO because it appears not to be in e-court yet, although it should be. By your leave, I'll read out what it says. It's the 1st Corps of the BH Army, Sarajevo, a command post in Sarajevo, Danijela Ozme Street, number 7, and then it lists the composition. They were brigades at the time. Does this appear to be the structure of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps? Does it seem similar, rather?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: This is a structure of a corps and laid out in a very similar manner to the nature of the chart of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. It appears to be a corps that is formed with a series of brigades, and at the bottom has an additional set of divisions which also appear to have then been subdivided into brigades.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification. Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I would note, Your Honour, that the original 65 ter number given by the accused was -- the last two numbers were flipped. It is, I believe, in e-court under 1D01829.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 29. Shall we check it first. Yes, we have it. Still missing is the English translation. So do we have the English translation, Mr. Hayden?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for the information. We'll mark it for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D307, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We agreed during our interview --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you know whose handwriting these are?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't. Evidently, it belongs to someone from the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We agreed that to the best of your knowledge, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps had up to 23.000 men; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: From one of the documents produced by the corps, itself, the establishment was shown to be at one point in time 23.000, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We agreed that only the command cadre were professionals, and not all of them, reserve officers or even ordinary privates, were in command posts; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Some of the posts within the Sarajevo Romanija Corps appear to have been occupied by reserve officers, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the corps, as a whole, did not have a sufficient number of trained officers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: That's a very difficult question for me to answer. It would depend on the activities of the corps. And as I haven't studied in detail what the corps was doing, I would not really be able to say whether it had sufficient officers to fulfill the tasks it was given. However, it appears to have had sufficiently well-trained officers for the purposes of command and control, and the purposes of passage of information from the front-line to the headquarters, and from the headquarters back to the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did we agree that apart from the high-ranking officers who were professionals, the other soldiers were not professionals, even though they had served in the JNA and were reservists after that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: The answer depends on your definition of a professional officer. Many of the officers in command posts, although not at that time full-time serving officers, had had full training within the JNA, and I suppose I would refer to the document we looked at earlier from the 1st Romanija Brigade up to the corps headquarters, stating that sufficiently well-trained officers were occupying the command posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Maybe that brigade, yes. But did you observe that this was not the case in all the brigades and it was not the case in the corps, as a whole?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: I don't have -- or I haven't seen a document -- all the documents from other brigades to the corps relating to this matter. There may be other documents, but if so, I haven't seen them. Many of the other officers in the other brigades appear to be JNA officers, but the only report that I've seen relating to capabilities and level of manning is the one from the 1st Romanija Brigade. That is to say, there may be other reports that I haven't seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree -- well, first of all, let's clear up a concept. In our language and in our system, a professional soldier is one who makes a living by being a soldier. Would you agree with that definition?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: It is, in a sense, a good distinction, "profession" meaning, let's call it, vocation. We're dealing with semantics here. In the British Army, you can be a professional soldier for just five years. You can be a full-time serving soldier for five years and then go into another occupation. You can be a part-time soldier, but that doesn't mean that you're less professional. It just means it's not your full-time occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that our reservists, both officers and privates, served in the JNA for nine months or a year, after which they were demobilised and did other jobs, but they were considered to be military conscripts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Again, I would have to qualify my answer. Having not studied the JNA, I'm not an expert on JNA training methods or even length of service. If you say they were trained for nine months or a year, then that is a relatively good period of time to train a soldier to a certain level. Does that answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mostly, yes. Do you agree, then, that some of them were occasionally summoned to manoeuvres once a year, the way it's done in your country?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: I would be assuming the answer to that question. I have no knowledge of it. I imagine that they had military training camps at different times during the year. Again, I'm not really the person to answer that question. I'm not an expert on the training regime of reservists from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this seem to be somewhat similar to your own system, when reservists take equipment home with them, and in our case they also took weapons home with them? We discussed this.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: In the British Army, a reservist is usually an ex-professional soldier who has left full-time service but then has a duty or can be recalled for service full time in the army at a later date. The other type of soldier in the British Army is a territorial army soldier, and he would not have served, necessarily, full-time in the army, but would have had part-time training, and he would be issued with kit and equipment, but not weapons, that he would keep with him at home. And he would then train at weekends or on certain weeks of the year and would also be eligible to be called up for service with the regular army, for example, in Afghanistan or Iraq nowadays. But I'm only -- my knowledge is of the British Army, not of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that a conscript in the JNA resembles a territorial army, as described by you, more than he resembles a soldier in Britain, would you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: I would have to compare the training of the two to see the level of training, so I couldn't give a comprehensive answer. Territorial army soldiers in the United Kingdom are trained to a very high level, and they do take part in combat activities, and they are currently serving in operations in Afghanistan. I don't know the level of training of a JNA conscript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a pity. It would be a good thing if you knew this, because it would make it easier for us to understand the structure of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. But if I tell you that army service lasted for a year, and later on nine months, that there were three or four months of intensive training and the rest was simply life in the barracks in an army unit, and after that people went back to their homes, to their regular work, and after that they were liable for military service and be called upon to attend training exercises, manoeuvres, or serve in case of a war, would that then resemble the description of a territorial army soldier in Britain, more than your professional soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: With the exception that territorial army soldiers are rarely trained continuously for three months. They normally are trained for two-week periods at a time and at weekends and on evenings. But with the description you have given, it would make a JNA reservist similar to a territorial army soldier in that respect, possibly even better trained, as they'd spent full time in the army for nine months.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please have 1D018935.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe we agreed yesterday that you knew a little bit about our territorial defence, which is a bit different from your territorial army. But its function is similar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: The British territorial army, the word "territorial" comes from the fact that units are recruited from a specific area or territory within the United Kingdom, but the unit is not expected to defend that area or to fight in that area. It could fight for national reasons, or be posted abroad, or be called up for humanitarian reasons. So there is no concept of territorial defence, in the Yugoslavian sense of the word. I have only read briefly of the concept of Tito -- of territorial defence, and by no means an expert on the concept of territorial defence. I understood it to be the defence of Yugoslavia against outside aggression, so that the entire country could defend itself against an aggressive act from outside Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in the Yugoslav Constitution, there was a ban on anyone signing an act of capitulation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that this meant that regardless of what the government did, every individual, wherever he found himself or herself, would have to oppose whoever was threatening the country --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Move on. Let's move on to the next question. Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm waiting for the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There's a slight mistake in the number. Is it 11835, 1D --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D01835. It was on the screen, but it was turned the wrong way. It has to be recalled on the screen. I'm not sure we have a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Philipps, this is dated the 26th of May in 1992. Do you remember that the JNA had to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina by the 20th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is dated the 26th of May, and it's an order issued by Tomislav Sipcic to establish a new Sarajevo brigade of territorial defence on the territory of Grbavica. The Blazuj Brigade was to be formed from the Territorial Defence of certain areas, and the Ilidza Brigade of Territorial Defence was to be formed from the territories of Dreoci, Vrelo Bosne, Ilidza, and Luzanj. These are the Serbian parts of Ilidza. The Kasindol Brigade of the Territorial Defence, the Rajlovac Brigade of the Territory Defence, the Vogosca Brigade of the Territorial Defence -- can we have the next page, please. So the Vogosca Brigade is the last one on this page, and then there's the Lukavica Brigade, the Pale Brigade, the Sokolac Brigade, the Rogatica Brigade, the Ilijas Brigade, and the Trnovo Brigade. Do you see that it was only on the 26th of May that steps were taken to form territorial units according to the municipalities from which they were being recruited and in which they would be active?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Yes, this seems to be an order to form brigades from territorial units.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D308, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In our interview, we agreed that the front-lines in Sarajevo were established according to neighbourhoods and that it didn't change much during the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: That's not precisely what was agreed, if that's the word to use. Many of the front-lines were established by the military situation; that is, the front-line came to be in a certain place because of the military activity that had taken place. Does that make sense to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But I'm interested in the point of time when the defence lines were being set up in particular neighbourhoods. Did we agree that these lines were not JNA lines, but lines of the local population?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: I don't really have enough knowledge of how the lines were set up in the first place. It seems that some of them were set up simply by people wanting to defend a particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree, and I think we did agree yesterday, that the military composition consisted of local men, people from the local population, who would go home after their shift; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: I haven't studied or looked at the home addresses or home towns of the individuals taking part within the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. I can only think of certain orders written by the corps commanders to try and prevent individual soldiers from returning home and fighting what was called a weekend war by the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were there in the year 2000. You visited Sarajevo on that year; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Yes, I was with SFOR for nine months in 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you ever find information or did you ever see any infrastructure, any barracks, where the men would be able to sleep, spend the night? For example, in Hadzici, in Vojkovici, in Ilijas, or anywhere else except for Lukavica, where the command was, was there any infrastructure, any dormitories for the men, or did they go home when their shift was over?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: My time in Sarajevo, of course, was spent working for SFOR, mostly relating to the implementation of the Dayton Agreement, and my task was as an intelligence staff officer. At that time, I was not certainly looking at matters relating to the battle for Sarajevo between 1992 and 1995, so I can't really comment on what barracks were there or had been built since, since SFOR, of course, had built barracks and were using barracks in and around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it seem self-evident to you that this was a peoples' army, who did not sleep in barracks but went to the front-line the way they would go to work, and then after work they would go home?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Again, a difficult question to answer, in that I haven't seen documents that relate to that matter. I certainly wouldn't expect soldiers on a front-line to expect to go home to sleep. Normally, in a static battle like that, soldiers would find a place on or near the front-line to spend the night. But, again, this is not an area of my expertise of how the war was conducted in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have we agreed that the Territorial Defence existed in municipalities, in local communes, and even in factories, and that these units of the Territorial Defence had their stockpiles of weapons?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Again, it's an area that I may have read about or heard people talk about, but it's not an area of expertise for me. I don't know what stockpiles of weapons existed or even if they existed, and I don't know enough about the organisation of the Territorial Defence to answer the level of command, if you like. I don't know whether it was at municipality level, or whether local communities had units, or whether factories had units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the Territorial Defence preceded all of these republican or -- yes, republican, newly-created armies, that they existed -- or, rather, that that existed as a structure and preceded everything that happened afterwards?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: As I understand it, the Territorial Defence was a concept set up by Tito. So, yes, the Territorial Defence existed before the transformation of the 4th Corps of the JNA into the SRK, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
